lesson.title: Counting Bytes, Not Packets: What TCP Sequence Numbers Really Track
lesson.summary: A TCP sequence number is the byte offset of a segment's first payload byte within the connection's overall stream, not a count of packets or segments, and that distinction is what makes reliable delivery possible.
lesson.body:
Every TCP segment header carries a 32 bit sequence number, one of the fields introduced in the previous chapter. It is tempting to think of it as a simple packet counter, segment one, segment two, segment three, but that is not what it is. A TCP sequence number is the byte offset of the first payload byte carried in that segment, counted from the connection's initial sequence number, the ISN chosen during the three way handshake.

The reason TCP counts bytes instead of segments is not a minor detail, it is what makes retransmission actually work. TCP is free to split or combine the byte stream into segments differently the second time around than it did the first, a retransmission might regroup data differently than the original transmission did, perhaps because the path's maximum segment size changed, or because two small writes that were sent separately the first time get combined into one segment on a retry. A counter based on segments would fall apart the moment segment boundaries shifted between the original send and a retransmission. A counter based on bytes never has that problem: no matter how the stream gets sliced into segments this time, every retransmission unambiguously identifies exactly which application bytes it is resending.

A worked example makes this precise. Continuing from the handshake example where the client's ISN was 1000, notice first that the SYN segment itself, despite carrying no application data, still consumes one sequence number, so the very first byte of real application data the client sends is numbered 1001, not 1000. Suppose the client then sends a 500 byte request in a single segment; that segment's sequence number is 1001, covering bytes 1001 through 1500. If the client later sends a 200 byte follow up, that next segment's sequence number is 1501, not simply 1002 or 2, because sequence numbers count cumulative bytes already sent in the stream, and 500 bytes were already consumed by the previous segment.

This exact numbering scheme is what makes the acknowledgment numbers in the next chapter meaningful in the first place: a receiver can say precisely "I have everything through byte 1500" only because sequence numbers describe a byte address space rather than an arbitrary packet identifier. The same scheme is also what lets a receiver detect exactly which bytes are missing when segments arrive out of order, and it is exactly what the TCP window, covered later, actually measures a range over.
